Bacterial Meningitis

On this page
Pyogenic infection of the leptomeninges and subarachnoid CSF — a true time-emergency where every hour to effective antibiotics + dexamethasone changes survival and neurologic outcome. Treat first, image/tap when safe.
Triad: fever + nuchal rigidity + altered mentation (all 3 in only ~44%) Target: door-to-antibiotics < 60 min Pneumococcal case-fatality ~20–30% Empiric: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (± Ampicillin if >50 / immunocompromised) + Dexamethasone Dx: lumbar puncture → CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, PCR
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Meningitis-causing bacteria first colonize the nasopharynx. In a susceptible host they breach the mucosa, enter the blood, and survive there because a polysaccharide capsule shields them from complement and phagocytes. Circulating bacteria then cross the blood–brain barrier (at the choroid plexus and cerebral microvasculature) and land in the subarachnoid space — an immune-privileged compartment with very little immunoglobulin or complement. With almost no local defense, they multiply freely.

The turning point is bacterial lysis: dying organisms shed cell-wall fragments (lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan) that ignite a host cytokine cascade — TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, chemokines and matrix metalloproteinases. This inflammation, not the bacteria directly, drives most of the damage: the blood–brain barrier becomes leaky, neutrophils pour in, and the brain develops vasogenic, cytotoxic and interstitial edema. Inflamed vessels thrombose (arteritis → infarction). The result is raised intracranial pressure, falling cerebral blood flow, ischemia and neuronal death — and the classic CSF signature of low glucose, high protein, high lactate and neutrophilic pleocytosis.

A fire in a sealed, unguarded vault. The subarachnoid space has almost no immune "guards," so the fire (bacteria) spreads unchecked. When you finally hit it with water (antibiotics), the sudden collapse throws up a cloud of smoke and steam (inflammatory debris) that swells the room — and because the skull can't expand, the pressure itself crushes the walls. That's why you dampen the smoke first (dexamethasone before/with the first antibiotic), not after.
Where each therapy acts on the cascade. Antibiotics stop bacterial replication; dexamethasone dampens the cytokine step that causes most brain injury (hence the timing); ICP measures counter the downstream edema. Diagram adapts to light/dark theme.
Thick purulent exudate blanketing the surface and sulci of the brain — the hallmark of pyogenic (pneumococcal) meningitis at autopsy.
Photo Credit: Content Providers(s): CDC/ Dr. Edwin P. Ewing, Jr. — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
CSF Gram stain: intracellular Gram-negative diplococci — Neisseria meningitidis. (Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci would suggest S. pneumoniae.)
Microman12345 — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
The through-line of this guide: antibiotics attack step ④ (kill the organism), dexamethasone attacks step ⑤ (blunt the cytokine storm — which is why it must precede or accompany the first antibiotic dose), and ICP-directed care attacks step ⑦ (edema and perfusion). Every drug below maps back to one of these steps.
🗂️

Classification — who grows what

By setting: Community-acquired vs Healthcare-associated (post-neurosurgical, post-traumatic, device/CSF-shunt–related, or nosocomial) — the latter shifts empiric coverage toward staphylococci and resistant Gram-negatives.

Age / hostMost likely pathogensEmpiric anchor
Neonate (0–1 mo)Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), E. coli / Gram-negatives, Listeria monocytogenesAmpicillin + cefotaxime (± gentamicin)
1 mo – 50 yS. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis; H. influenzae if unvaccinatedVancomycin + ceftriaxone
> 50 y+ Listeria, aerobic Gram-negative bacilliVancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin
Immunocompromised
HIV, transplant, steroids, biologics		+ Listeria, Gram-negatives (incl. Pseudomonas), Cryptococcus, TBVancomycin + ampicillin + cefepime/meropenem
Basilar skull fracture / CSF leakS. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, group A strepVancomycin + ceftriaxone
Post-neurosurgery · penetrating trauma · CSF shuntStaphylococci (incl. MRSA / CoNS), aerobic Gram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas, CutibacteriumVancomycin + cefepime or ceftazidime or meropenem

Case-fatality (treated, adults): pneumococcal ~20–30% · meningococcal ~3–10% (higher with fulminant meningococcemia) · Listeria ~15–30% · Gram-negative bacillary highest. Long-term sequelae (esp. hearing loss, cognitive deficits) affect up to a third of survivors.

Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Presentation — symptoms & signs by frequency

Bacterial meningitis rarely "lives" in clinic — but it often walks in as a headache-and-fever visit. The job here is pattern recognition and a low threshold to send to the ED. Frequencies below are for adults (symptom frequencies: van de Beek et al., NEJM 2004; meningeal-sign sensitivities: Thomas et al., CID 2002).

>70% 40–70% 15–40% <15%
Symptom / sign~FreqWhy it happens
Headache~87%Inflamed meninges stretch pain-sensitive dura & vessels; rising ICP
Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity)~83%Meningeal irritation → reflex paraspinal spasm resisting neck flexion
Fever ≥38 °C~77%Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) reset the hypothalamic set-point
Nausea / vomiting~74%Raised ICP & meningeal irritation stimulate the area postrema
≥2 of 4 cardinal features~95%Headache, fever, neck stiffness, or ↓mentation — the practical rule-in screen; near-absence argues strongly against
Altered mental status (GCS <14)~69%Cortical dysfunction from edema, ↓cerebral blood flow, cytokines, ± seizures
Photophobia~45%Trigeminal / meningeal sensitization
Classic triad (fever + neck stiffness + AMS)~44%All three coincide in <½ of cases — its absence does not exclude meningitis
Focal neurologic deficit~30%Cranial neuropathies (esp. CN VI, VIII), arteritic infarction, mass effect
Petechial / purpuric rash~26%Meningococcal endotoxin → DIC & dermal microthrombi; seen in >50% of meningococcemia
Seizure at / before presentation~15–25%Cortical irritation, infarction, hyponatremia; commoner with pneumococcus
Papilledema~3–5%Sustained raised ICP — a late sign, often absent even when ICP is high
Non-blanching petechiae / purpura — treat as meningococcemia until proven otherwise: droplet precautions, notify public health, prophylax close contacts.

Meningeal exam signs — rule-in, never rule-out

SignHow to elicitSens.Spec.Use it for
Nuchal rigidityPassive neck flexion is resisted~30%~68%Best of the three, still misses many
Kernig signHip flexed 90° → knee extension resisted/painful~5%~95%Rule-in only
Brudzinski signPassive neck flexion → involuntary hip/knee flexion~5%~95%Rule-in only
Jolt accentuationHeadache worsens on 2–3 Hz horizontal head rotation~21%lowDo NOT use to exclude meningitis
Normal meningeal signs do not rule out bacterial meningitis (Kernig/Brudzinski sensitivity ~5%). If the story fits — fever + headache/AMS — tap and treat, don't lean on the exam.

Who is at higher risk

  • Immunocompromise: HIV, transplant, chronic steroids/biologics, diabetes, chronic kidney/liver disease, malignancy
  • Asplenia / hyposplenia and complement (C5–C9) deficiency or eculizumab/ravulizumab use → encapsulated organisms; meningococcus can be fulminant & recurrent
  • Anatomic: CSF leak / basilar skull fracture, cochlear implant, prior neurosurgery or CSF shunt
  • Exposure/host: crowding (dorms, military), close contact of a case, alcohol use disorder, pregnancy & age >50 (both raise Listeria risk), unvaccinated
Act now

First moves & differential

🚨

Don't work it up in clinic — move it

Suspected bacterial meningitis = activate EMS / send to the ED now. Diagnostic workup (LP, CT, blood cultures) belongs in the ED and must not delay antibiotics. There is no outpatient version of this disease.
If transfer to definitive care will be delayed (>30–60 min) or the patient looks septic / has a non-blanching petechial-purpuric rash → give empiric parenteral antibiotics before transfer (e.g., ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM; benzylpenicillin is an alternative for suspected meningococcal disease). Draw blood cultures only if it takes seconds — never hold antibiotics for them. Document the time given.
Time is brainObservational cohorts link every hour of delay to effective antibiotics with worse survival and neurologic outcome — the pre-hospital/first-contact clinician's job is speed and antibiotics, not certainty.

Differential — what else mimics it

ConsiderCluesHow to separate it
Viral (aseptic) meningitisLess toxic, mentation intact, enterovirus seasonCSF lymphocytic, normal glucose; enterovirus PCR; usually self-limited
HSV / viral encephalitisProminent AMS, behavioral change, seizures, focal deficitMRI temporal lobe, CSF HSV PCR → add empiric acyclovir if suspected
Subarachnoid hemorrhageThunderclap "worst headache of life," sudden onsetNon-contrast CT; LP xanthochromia if CT negative & >6 h
Brain abscess / subdural empyemaFocal deficit, subacute, sinus/ear/dental sourceContrast MRI; LP may be contraindicated (mass effect)
Subacute meningitidesDays–weeks, immunosuppressed, exposuresTB, cryptococcal, Lyme, syphilis, carcinomatous — targeted CSF studies
Drug-induced aseptic meningitisRecent NSAID, TMP-SMX, IVIGDiagnosis of exclusion; resolves on withdrawal
Treat

Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts

💊

Meningococcal & Hib — protect the exposed

Who is a "close contact" of meningococcal disease? Household members; child-care / preschool contacts; and anyone directly exposed to the patient's oral/respiratory secretions (kissing, mouth-to-mouth, unprotected intubation/suctioning) during the 7 days before onset until 24 h of effective therapy. Give prophylaxis ASAP (ideally <24 h); it adds little >14 days out. Casual school/work and most healthcare contacts do not need it.
DrugStart / doseCourseWhy / how it worksCautions & alternatives
Ceftriaxone250 mg IM ×1 (125 mg if <15 y)Single doseEradicates nasopharyngeal carriage; preferred in pregnancyReliable where cipro resistance exists
Ciprofloxacin500 mg PO ×1Single doseOne-and-done oral option for adultsAvoid where cipro-resistant meningococcus circulates (CDC 2024) — use rifampin, ceftriaxone, or azithromycin
Rifampin600 mg PO q12h (peds 10 mg/kg q12h)2 days (4 doses)Penetrates respiratory mucosa; clears carriageCYP inducer (↓OCP, warfarin, many drugs); orange secretions/soft-lens staining; avoid in pregnancy
Azithromycin500 mg PO ×1Single doseOral alternative; useful in cipro-resistant areasReasonable when the above are unsuitable
The index patient also needs carriage eradication before discharge unless treated with ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (which already clear it) — penicillin and some other regimens do not.
Hib prophylaxisFor H. influenzae type b disease: rifampin 20 mg/kg (max 600 mg) PO once daily × 4 days for household contacts when there is an unvaccinated/incompletely-vaccinated child <4 y or an immunocompromised child in the home.

Meningococcal and Hib disease are reportable — notify the local health department, which coordinates contact tracing and outbreak response.

Monitor

After recovery — follow-up

📈

Surveillance for sequelae

AudiologyFormal hearing test within 4 weeks of discharge — sensorineural hearing loss is the most common sequela (CN VIII / cochlear injury). If profound loss and a cochlear implant is considered, refer urgently before labyrinthine ossification sets in.≤4 wk
Neuro / cognitiveReassess for focal deficits, cognitive slowing, mood, and (in children) development. Refer to neuro-rehab for persistent deficits.Follow-up
Seizure careIf seizures occurred acutely, arrange neurology follow-up; most acute symptomatic seizures don't need lifelong AEDs.If applicable
Host work-upRecurrent, unusual, or serogroup-atypical disease → evaluate for complement deficiency, asplenia, HIV, and CSF leak; complete indicated vaccines.Selected
Steroids reduce hearing loss but don't eliminate it — every bacterial-meningitis survivor gets a hearing test, even if they seem fine.
Prevent

Vaccination & prevention

🛡️

ACIP / CDC — the real prevention lever

There is no USPSTF screening test for meningitis — prevention is vaccination (ACIP/CDC) plus recognizing high-risk hosts. Conjugate vaccines have made S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis the dominant adult pathogens and nearly eliminated H. influenzae type b.

VaccineWho / when (ACIP)Covers
MenACWY (conjugate)Routine at 11–12 y with a booster at 16 y; plus high-risk groups (below) & first-year college students in dorms, travelers to the meningitis belt / Hajj, microbiologists, outbreaksSerogroups A, C, W, Y
MenBShared clinical decision-making, ages 16–23 (preferred 16–18); routine for high-risk groupsSerogroup B
MenABCWY (pentavalent)
Penbraya / Penmenvy		May be given when both MenACWY and MenB are due at the same visit (≥10 y at increased risk; healthy 16–23 y via SCDM) — 2023–2025 ACIPA, B, C, W, Y
Pneumococcal conjugate
PCV15 / PCV20 / PCV21		All adults ≥50 y (lowered from 65 in 2024) and 19–49 y with risk conditions; routine childhood seriesS. pneumoniae
PPSV23After PCV15 in selected patients (not needed after PCV20/PCV21)S. pneumoniae
Hib conjugateRoutine infant series; catch-up for asplenia, HSCT, certain immunodeficienciesH. influenzae type b
Complement inhibitors (eculizumab / ravulizumab) raise meningococcal risk ~1000–2000× even after vaccination — give MenACWY + MenB and antibacterial prophylaxis (e.g., penicillin) while on therapy. Asplenia / hyposplenia: ensure pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccination — encapsulated organisms can be fulminant.
Escalate

When to send to the ED — now

🚑

Red flags → call 911 / ED

  • Fever + headache with neck stiffness, photophobia, or altered mentation
  • Any non-blanching petechial / purpuric rash with fever → possible meningococcemia — 911
  • New confusion, drowsiness, seizure, or focal neurologic deficit with fever
  • Rapidly progressive illness, toxic appearance, hypotension, or mottling
  • Immunocompromised / asplenic / complement-deficient patient with fever + headache — very low threshold
  • Signs of raised ICP: severe headache with vomiting, new bradycardia + hypertension, papilledema
If transfer will be delayed or the patient looks septic / has purpura, give ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM before transfer and document the time. Antibiotics first — certainty later.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Admit everyone — then move fast

📋

The first hour & who goes to the ICU

Every patient with suspected acute bacterial meningitis is admitted. The only triage decision is floor vs ICU — and it does not delay the first-hour bundle.

First-hour bundle — blood cultures ×2 → dexamethasone → empiric antibiotics within 60 min of arrival → LP when safe. Give steroids before/with the first antibiotic dose. If a CT is needed first, treat, then scan, then tap.
The meningitis clock. Antibiotics are the one step that cannot wait; imaging and the tap fit around them.
Straight to ICU if any of: GCS ≤ 12 (or a drop ≥ 2), need for airway protection (GCS ≤ 8), septic shock / vasopressor need, respiratory failure, status epilepticus or recurrent seizures, signs of raised ICP or herniation, or rapidly spreading purpura / DIC. Everything else → floor with close neuro checks. Full thresholds in "When to call ICU."

🧪

What to order

Blood cultures ×2Before antibiotics only if it takes seconds; positive in ~50–90% and often salvage the microbiology when the LP is delayed or partially treated.Now
CBC, CMP, glucose, coags, lactateBaseline; a paired serum glucose is required to read the CSF:serum ratio; check platelets/INR before LP.Now

🧭

Lumbar puncture & the CT-before-LP decision

Antibiotics + dexamethasone come before the scan when a CT is indicated — the tap can wait, the drugs cannot.
LP cautions: hold/defer for clinical signs of impending herniation (not merely a "normal" CT), platelets <~50k or coagulopathy (correct first), or skin infection over the site. A normal head CT does not rule out dangerously raised ICP — the clinical herniation exam does.

*Very early viral meningitis can be neutrophil-predominant. Prior antibiotics lower Gram-stain and culture yield and can partially normalize cell counts — but glucose/protein and PCR still help. Spanos/Hoen individual predictors of bacterial meningitis (~99% certainty): CSF:serum glucose ≤0.23, CSF protein ≥220 mg/dL, CSF WBC ≥2000/µL, or CSF neutrophils ≥1180/µL — any one alone is enough to commit to bacterial therapy.

Treat

Antibiotics & dexamethasone

💊

Empiric → targeted — the ladder

Antibiotics kill the organism (cascade step ④); dexamethasone blunts the cytokine surge those dying bacteria trigger (step ⑤) — which is exactly why steroids go in before or with the first antibiotic dose, not after. Doses below are for adults with normal renal function; IDSA total daily doses in parentheses.
1
Empiric therapy + dexamethasone — within 60 min
Cover pneumococcus + meningococcus (+ Listeria in at-risk hosts); dampen inflammation.
▾
DrugDose (start)Interval / total dailyWhy it's in the regimenIf allergic / alternative
Dexamethasone0.15 mg/kg (≈10 mg) IVq6h × 2–4 d — 10–20 min before / with 1st abxBlunts TNF-α/IL-1 injury; ↓mortality & hearing loss (esp. pneumococcal)Continue only for pneumococcus (ESCMID: ± H. flu); stop otherwise
Ceftriaxone2 g IVq12h (4 g/day)Kills pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. flu, most GNR; penetrates inflamed meningesCefotaxime 2 g q4–6h; severe β-lactam allergy → aztreonam/moxifloxacin + vancomycin (meropenem often tolerated)
Vancomycin15–20 mg/kg IV
(load 25–30 mg/kg)		q8–12h; trough 15–20 µg/mL (30–45 mg/kg/day)Covers cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae until susceptibilities returnLinezolid or daptomycin if true intolerance (limited CNS data) — check levels
Ampicillin
add if >50 y / immunocompromised / pregnant / alcoholic		2 g IVq4h (12 g/day)Adds Listeria cover — cephalosporins do not kill ListeriaPenicillin allergy → TMP-SMX 5 mg/kg (TMP) q6–8h for Listeria; desensitize/consult
Acyclovir
if HSV encephalitis can't be excluded		10 mg/kg IVq8h until HSV ruled outCovers HSV when early features overlap with meningitisn/a — hydrate, monitor renal function
Post-neurosurgical / penetrating trauma / CSF-shunt or -drain (IDSA 2017): vancomycin + an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam — cefepime 2 g q8h, ceftazidime 2 g q8h, or meropenem 2 g q8h. β-lactam anaphylaxis → aztreonam or ciprofloxacin. Remove/externalize infected hardware.
Dexamethasone — the rulesGive before/with the first antibiotic (much less effective afterward). Continue only if pneumococcus is confirmed (Gram-positive diplococci or S. pneumoniae on culture; ESCMID also continues for H. influenzae) — stop for Listeria, meningococcus, or a non-bacterial diagnosis. Benefit is concentrated in pneumococcal disease / high-income settings; it was not beneficial in high-HIV, resource-limited trials.
2

Once Gram stain / culture / PCR return — narrow and set the duration.

De-escalation rules: stop vancomycin once pneumococcus proves ceftriaxone-susceptible; stop ampicillin if no Listeria; stop dexamethasone if the organism isn't pneumococcus (± H. flu). Confirm renal-adjusted doses.
3
Resistance, allergy & when to re-tap
Refractory / special situations.
▾
  • Severe β-lactam allergy: confirm the reaction; many "penicillin-allergic" patients tolerate meropenem/ceftriaxone. True anaphylaxis → aztreonam or a fluoroquinolone (GNR) + vancomycin ± TMP-SMX (Listeria); consider desensitization.
  • Highly resistant pneumococcus: keep vancomycin + ceftriaxone; add rifampin if delayed response and ceftriaxone MIC ≥2 (never rifampin monotherapy).
  • Repeat LP at 24–48 h if: no clinical improvement, resistant pneumococcus on dexamethasone, Gram-negative bacillary meningitis, or a neonate.
  • Device-related (IDSA 2017): systemic therapy ± intraventricular antibiotics (vancomycin 5–20 mg or an aminoglycoside) when the response is poor; clamp the drain 15–60 min after instillation.
🔗

Comorbidity interactions — how they change the plan

ComorbidityEffect on pathogens / courseWhat changes in management
HIV / immunocompromise+ Listeria, GNR, Cryptococcus, TB; atypical presentationsAdd ampicillin; send CrAg/AFB; low threshold for antivirals/antifungals
Age > 50 / pregnancy / alcohol useListeria risk risesAdd ampicillin (± gentamicin); pregnancy → avoid unnecessary fluoroquinolones
Asplenia / hypospleniaFulminant encapsulated organismsDon't wait — treat fast; vaccinate on recovery
Complement deficiency / eculizumabRecurrent, sometimes atypical meningococcusVaccinate + antibacterial prophylaxis; evaluate complement
CSF leak / basilar skull fx / cochlear implantRecurrent pneumococcal meningitisPneumococcal vaccine; ENT/neurosurgical repair of the defect
Renal impairmentDrug accumulationDose-adjust vancomycin, cephalosporins, meropenem, acyclovir; follow levels
Epilepsy on valproateSeizure riskMeropenem drops valproate levels → breakthrough seizures; use an alternative AED
Diabetes+ GNR, pneumococcus; hyperglycemiaGlucose control; remember serum glucose skews the CSF:serum ratio
Drugs / moves to avoid:
  • Never delay antibiotics for CT or LP — the single most important error.
  • Cephalosporins alone miss Listeria — always add ampicillin in at-risk hosts.
  • No aminoglycoside monotherapy — poor CSF penetration.
  • Ceftriaxone in neonates — bilirubin displacement (kernicterus) & IV-calcium precipitation → use cefotaxime.
  • Dexamethasone lowers vancomycin CSF penetration — dose vancomycin adequately, follow levels, consider rifampin if not improving.
  • Avoid hypotonic fluids / reflexive fluid restriction — keep euvolemia; hyponatremia is common but don't dry out a hypovolemic patient.
  • Ciprofloxacin prophylaxis where cipro-resistant meningococcus circulates (CDC 2024).

⚠️

Anticipate, don't react

ComplicationClueAction

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

Neuro checksGCS, pupils, focal signs q1–4h early — any deterioration → repeat imaging & escalate. This is the highest-yield "vital sign."q1–4h
SodiumDaily (often twice-daily early) — SIADH and cerebral salt wasting are common; volume status separates them.Daily
Renal function + drug levelsCreatinine for renal-adjusted dosing; vancomycin trough/AUC; CBC (cytopenias).Daily
Micro resultsChase Gram stain → culture → susceptibilities → de-escalate; confirm blood-culture clearance.Ongoing
Source huntLook for a parameningeal focus — sinusitis, otitis/mastoiditis, endocarditis, CSF leak; involve ENT/ID.Early
Infection control & public healthDroplet precautions for 24 h of effective therapy (meningococcus/Hib); notify public health & arrange contact prophylaxis.Day 1
Most patients defervesce and improve neurologically within 48–72 h. Failure to improve is a prompt to re-image, re-tap, hunt a parameningeal source, and re-check susceptibilities — not to simply "wait longer."
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Concrete escalation thresholds

TriggerThresholdWhy / what it needs
Depressed consciousnessGCS ≤ 12 or a drop ≥ 2 pointsFrequent neuro checks; imaging; possible ICP monitoring
Airway at riskGCS ≤ 8, loss of gag, apneaIntubate for airway protection
ShockSBP < 90 / MAP < 65 after ≥ 30 mL/kg crystalloidVasopressors, central access, arterial line
Respiratory failureSpO₂ < 92% on O₂, RR > 30, rising PaCO₂Support / intubation
SeizuresStatus epilepticus or recurrent seizuresContinuous therapy ± cEEG
Raised ICP / herniationFixed/unequal pupils, Cushing triad, posturing, deteriorating papilledemaEmergency osmotherapy + neurosurgery / ICP monitor
Fulminant meningococcemiaRapidly spreading purpura, DICICU sepsis care, correct coagulopathy
Severe hyponatremiaNa < 125 mmol/L or rapidly falling + symptomsClose monitoring, careful correction
When in doubt, call early. Neurologic deterioration in meningitis can be swift, and the interventions that matter (airway, osmotherapy, ICP monitoring) are unit-level.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile trend (or a clear explanation), stable/improving neuro exam, tolerating orals; organism-directed therapy with a defined duration underway (IV completion arranged via OPAT/PICC if needed); complications controlled (no active seizures, ICP settled, sodium stable); audiology booked; rehab needs assessed; and public-health/contact tasks done.

Home

Back to neurologic baseline, orals fine, reliable follow-up; finishing an oral or short course with audiology scheduled.

Home health / OPAT

Needs to complete IV antibiotics at home (once-daily ceftriaxone is OPAT-friendly) via PICC + nursing.

SNF

Needs 24h skilled nursing / IV therapy, deconditioned, <3h therapy/day tolerance.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Meaningful motor/cognitive deficits but can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care — ventilator weaning, complicated ventriculitis, long unstable IV courses.

Hospice / palliative

Devastating neurologic injury; comfort-focused, goals-of-care aligned.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Bacterial meningitis earns an ICU bed for brain and/or hemodynamic failure: depressed or fluctuating consciousness (GCS ≤ 12, airway risk at ≤ 8), septic shock, respiratory failure, status epilepticus, or signs of raised ICP / herniation. Rapidly spreading purpura (meningococcemia) is an ICU disease until proven otherwise.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

Arterial line, central access, what to trend.

Support

ICP, seizures & hemodynamics

💉

Protect the brain, hold the pressure

1
Raised-ICP ladder
Escalate tier by tier.
▾
  • Tier 0: head of bed 30° & midline, treat fever/pain/agitation, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40), normo/hypertonic sodium, avoid hypotension.
  • Tier 1 — hyperosmolar therapy: hypertonic saline 3% 250 mL bolus (or 23.4% 30 mL via central line) or mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV; follow Na (goal up to ~150–155), osmolality/osmolar gap.
  • Tier 2: deepen sedation/analgesia; CSF drainage via EVD if hydrocephalus/monitor in place.
  • Tier 3 — herniation bridge only: brief hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 30–35 as a temporary measure to the OR; not prophylactic (causes ischemia).
  • Tier 4: neuromuscular blockade, decompressive surgery; barbiturate coma as a last resort.
2
Seizure control
They raise ICP and metabolic demand.
▾

Active seizure: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (4 mg, may repeat). Load an AED: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg) or fosphenytoin 20 PE/kg. Refractory / status: continuous midazolam or propofol infusion with cEEG. Avoid meropenem in patients on valproate.

3
Septic shock / Waterhouse-Friderichsen
Keep MAP up to protect cerebral perfusion.
▾
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ > β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line — supports MAP → CPP
VasopressinV₁ receptors0.03 units/min (fixed)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd-on to norepinephrine
Epinephrineβ₁ = α₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO & SVRRefractory shock
HydrocortisoneGlucocorticoid50 mg IV q6hRestores vascular tonePressor-refractory shock / suspected adrenal failure (W-F)
In meningitis the pressor goal isn't just organ perfusion — a decent MAP is what keeps CPP (= MAP − ICP) above the ischemia threshold when ICP is high. Fulminant meningococcemia can also cause adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen), so add stress-dose hydrocortisone when shock is refractory.
Airway

Respiratory support & vent

🌬️

NIV vs intubate; initial settings

Intubate for airway protection when GCS ≤ 8, the gag is lost, there are recurrent seizures, or for refractory shock/respiratory failure. Non-invasive ventilation is generally inappropriate — depressed consciousness means aspiration risk. Use a smooth induction (pre-treat to blunt the ICP surge) and keep the head up.

Do not prophylactically hyperventilate — dropping PaCO₂ constricts cerebral vessels and can cause ischemia. Reserve brief hyperventilation (PaCO₂ 30–35) as a bridge for acute herniation only.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When the standard ladder fails

  • Refractory raised ICP: external ventricular drain (also treats hydrocephalus), decompressive craniectomy, deep sedation + neuromuscular blockade, barbiturate coma (last resort).
  • Refractory seizures / NCSE: continuous midazolam or propofol infusions titrated to cEEG; add a maintenance AED.
  • Ventriculitis / shunt infection: systemic + intraventricular antibiotics (vancomycin 5–20 mg or an aminoglycoside; IDSA 2017), externalize/remove hardware, clamp drain 15–60 min after instillation.
  • Refractory septic shock: add vasopressin/epinephrine, stress-dose hydrocortisone; correct DIC/coagulopathy.
Therapeutic (induced) hypothermia is NOT recommended in adult bacterial meningitis — the randomized trial (Mourvillier, JAMA 2013) was stopped early for a signal of harm. Control fever, but don't cool below normothermia.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Ready for the floor when all hold: off vasopressors ≥ 24 h & hemodynamically stable · extubated and protecting the airway · GCS ≥ 13 / improving and stable neuro exam · no seizures ≥ 24–48 h on a stable regimen · ICP controlled with EVD removed or stable (no herniation risk) · on definitive organism-directed antibiotics with the source addressed.
Not yet if: consciousness is still fluctuating, seizures are ongoing, ICP or pressor requirements are climbing, or sodium is unstable — these predict a bounce-back.
Pearls

High-yield pearls

💡

The 15 things to actually remember

  1. Treat first, tap when safe. Blood cultures → dexamethasone → antibiotics within 60 min. If a CT is needed, treat before you scan.
  2. Dexamethasone goes in before/with the first antibiotic — it barely helps once bacteria have already lysed. Continue only for pneumococcus (ESCMID: ± H. influenzae).
  3. The classic triad is present in only ~44%, but ~95% have ≥2 of fever, headache, neck stiffness, or altered mentation — near-absence of all four argues strongly against.
  4. Kernig/Brudzinski sensitivity is ~5% — never rule out meningitis on the exam; jolt accentuation is also unreliable (~21%).
  5. Petechiae/purpura = meningococcemia until proven otherwise → droplet precautions, notify public health, prophylax contacts.
  6. Add ampicillin for Listeria in age >50, pregnancy, alcohol use, or immunocompromise — cephalosporins don't cover it.
  7. Vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus, but dexamethasone reduces its CSF penetration — dose adequately, follow levels, add rifampin if the response lags.
  8. CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 beats the absolute glucose. Spanos predictors (ratio ≤0.23, protein ≥220, WBC ≥2000, or PMN ≥1180) each predict bacterial at ~99%.
  9. CSF lactate is sensitive (~98%) only if antibiotic-naïve — it falls to ~49% after antibiotics.
  10. A normal CT does not exclude raised ICP — the clinical herniation exam is the LP contraindication, not the scan.
  11. Repeat the LP at 24–48 h if there's no improvement, resistant pneumococcus on steroids, Gram-negative meningitis, or a neonate.
  12. Give empiric acyclovir when you can't exclude HSV encephalitis early — you often can't tell them apart at hour one.
  13. Meningococcal & Hib are reportable; use droplet precautions for 24 h of therapy, and eradicate carriage in the index patient unless a cephalosporin was used.
  14. Don't over-restrict fluids. Keep euvolemia; hyponatremia (SIADH/cerebral salt wasting) is common but drying out a hypovolemic patient worsens perfusion.
  15. Every survivor gets a hearing test within 4 weeks — sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest sequela — and no therapeutic hypothermia (JAMA 2013 stopped for harm).
